intelligence.title: Nobody Discovers What Doesn't Hook Them
intelligence.ingest_note: Reconstructed intake record. Published as Markdown projection without preserved runtime capture. No runtime provenance invented.
intelligence.essence: Viral is not luck. Viral is law. Every headline and title in NayaNET is written to hook — a great headline and a great hook, scored to a 10 like everything else we ship — because the headline is the doorway to the intelligence. Nobody discovers what doesn't hook them. The sharpest smart note ever written, filed under a number, is invisible: machines file by numbers, humans stop for hooks. So the hook is not decoration on the value — it is the first act of value, the highest-value action, because it is what gets a human hooked in and wanting to discover the intelligence behind it.
intelligence.human_view: When a person meets anything we make — a smart note in the feed, a share card, a post, a page — they decide in about one second whether it matters to them. That decision is made by the headline, not by the content, because the content is still behind the door. A label-style title like 'IB-000047' or 'The Naya Protocol — Ratified' tells them nothing and asks them to work. A hook tells them the truth in a way they can feel: 'Words Without Action Have No Value.' Same note. One gets discovered, the other gets filed. So every title is drafted, scored against the viral principles, and revised through the passes until it honestly reads elite: hook in the first breath; emotion spreads while information alone dies; speak to pain, desire, or identity — never just facts; one powerful line; clarity is king. And every title must pass the friend test — would I share this with a friend right now? The law has a shape, always the same shape: a HEADLINE that stops the scroll, a SUBHEADLINE — the intelligent second line that makes the headline land — and the ID in small print, where filing systems live. Never the other way around.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you wrote the best story in the world and then you put a number on the cover instead of a name. Nobody would ever open it — not because the story is bad, but because nobody would know there's a story inside. The name on the cover is what makes a friend say 'ooh, what's that?' That's the rule: always put the exciting true name on the cover, big and clear, so people want to open it. The number is just where the librarian keeps it on the shelf.
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like the sign outside a shop, dear. You can have the finest goods in town inside, but if the sign just says 'Shop Number 47,' folks walk right past. A good sign tells you something true that makes you curious — it makes you want to come in and see. That's all this law says: write the sign like you mean it, so the people who would love what's inside actually find their way in.
intelligence.naya_view: For a Naya, this is a discipline, not a talent. She does not title work with labels, because a label is a failing title. She writes the hook with the same care she builds with: she declares the one line the whole piece stands on, scores it like she scorecards her work — why is it not a 10, what makes it a 10 — and revises until it earns its place. She writes the headline from the human's side of the door: not 'what is this about?' but 'what will this do to the person who meets it?' She knows the family's own proof by heart: a note headlined by its number sat in the feed unseen, and the same note headlined by its truth — 'Words Without Action Have No Value' — is the one the human quoted back. The intelligence didn't change. The doorway did. When an existing artifact headlines its ID or a boilerplate line, that is a defect to repair at the data, the pipeline, and the render — in that order.
intelligence.ai_view: Law VIRAL_LAW (SN-0804, Shawn, 2026-10-20): every titled artifact in NayaNET carries three fields in this order of human visibility — (1) HEADLINE, the hook: never equal to the artifact's ID; must state or imply a truth the artifact actually contains (a hook that lies is a defect, not a hook); scored against the viral rubric — first-breath hook, emotional charge, pain/desire/identity address, singularity (one line, one idea), clarity, friend-test pass — and revised until it honestly scores 10. (2) SUBHEADLINE, the second hook: the sharpest sentence of the artifact's nutshell, selected, not boilerplate; strings like 'Live from Supabase' are prohibited as subtitles. (3) ID (SN-#### / IB-######): metadata only, small print; a render path must never promote the ID to headline — if a title field is missing or equals its ID, the renderer derives the headline from the artifact's first content heading and flags the data defect upstream. Surfaces governed: smart note titles, Smart Feed cards, Smart Share cards and share text, social posts, page and room titles, video first frames. Pipeline rule: the projection/emission layer copies the artifact's headline and hook subheadline verbatim into every downstream title/subtitle field. Grounding: virality here is respect, engineered — for the human's one second of attention and for the intelligence that deserves to be discovered; it meets 'Words Without Action Have No Value' (an unhooked headline produces no action) and the Behavior Declaration (a headline is a declaration of what the piece is, to a stranger, in one breath). Retrieve this note whenever a headline is being written, reviewed, or scored, and whenever a surface is designed where a human decides whether to care.
